ENT Clinical Note – Telephone Encounter  

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure  
  • 4–5-day history of “cough and cold,” feeling run-down. Began after dinner out on Saturday; no clear food / drug / environmental trigger identified.  
- Symptom timeline and progression  
  • Day 1: onset of cough (mainly dry), runny nose, malaise; one episode of diarrhoea.  
  • Days 2-5: persistent cough with occasional “mucky” sputum, sore throat, audible sniffles, subjective fevers/rigors with night sweats, increasing shortness of breath (described as “not good”), generalized myalgias/joint stiffness.  
- ENT symptoms  
  • Throat: mild sore throat; transient hoarseness attributed to shouting; no throat-closing sensation, dysphagia, odynophagia, or drooling.  
  • Nasal/ocular: continuous runny nose/sniffles; no ocular itching/tearing reported.  
  • Ear: mild blocked/dull sensation, no significant pain or hearing loss.  
  • Airway: no stridor, noisy breathing, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling.  
  • Neck: no pain or swelling.  
- Relevant past episodes/treatments: none; first episode of this kind.  
- Allergies & current medications  
  • Allergies: none known.  
  • Medications: Metformin (dose not documented), Lisinopril (dose not documented), PRN aspirin (dose/freq not documented).  
- Social context: Lives with wife; children grown and out of home.

Objective (telephone assessment):
- Observable swelling: none noted.  
- Airway/breathing: patient speaking in full sentences; reports dyspnoea but no audible stridor or wheeze.  
- Nasal: audible congestion/sniffles.  
- Mental status: alert, conversational; no dizziness or syncope reported.  
- Vitals & physical exam: Not recorded (telephone encounter).  
- Accompaniment: Wife at home (implied).

Assessment:
Suspected acute viral upper respiratory infection / influenza-like illness (incl. possible COVID-19); need to rule out early community-acquired pneumonia.  
Evidence: 4–5-day course of cough, rhinorrhoea, sore throat, myalgias, subjective fever, shortness of breath, brief GI upset; no focal chest pain; examination unavailable.  

Top aligned differential diagnoses (per DDx):  
1. Acute viral URTI / influenza-like illness – high likelihood: classic constellation of upper-airway and systemic symptoms.  
2. Community-acquired pneumonia – medium likelihood: productive cough, dyspnoea, subjective fever; objective findings lacking.  
3. Acute bronchitis – medium likelihood: sub-acute cough after URI; overlaps with above; usually self-limiting.  
No transcript–DDx conflicts noted.

Plan:
- Provided delayed prescription: Amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID ×5 days; patient to start only if symptoms persist or worsen after 24–48 h.  
- Symptomatic management: rest, adequate hydration, regular Paracetamol for fever/pain.  
- Patient instructions / red flags: seek urgent care (GP, ED, or call emergency services) for:  
  • Worsening dyspnoea or inability to speak full sentences  
  • New chest pain, persistent high fever or rigors  
  • Confusion, dizziness, collapse  
  • Any throat swelling, voice change, drooling, or difficulty swallowing  
- Follow-up: Re-evaluate (telephone or in-person) if not improved within one week or sooner if concerned; consider in-office vitals, chest and ENT exam, and COVID-19 testing.  
- Preventive/long-term: encourage continued smoking cessation (vaping transition), moderate alcohol intake, and adherence to diabetes/HTN management.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing but clinically expected: objective vitals (T°, HR, RR, BP, SpO₂); physical chest/ENT exam; COVID-19 test and vaccination status; exact doses of Metformin and Lisinopril.  
● Transcript–DDx conflicts: none.  
● Transcript quality: clear overall; minor conversational digressions, but clinical content intelligible.
